cards.explanation: The answer is whoever surrenders to the Chaldeans. Jeremiah the prophet says the LORD's word is “…whoever surrenders to the Chaldeans will live…” (Jeremiah 38:2). I know, I know, friends, surrender is not the sermon anybody wants to hear. But it's the one the text gives.

The answer is False. Jeremiah says the LORD's word is, “This city will surely be delivered into the hands of the army of the king of Babylon, and he will capture it.” (Jeremiah 38:3). The word is not that Babylon will fail. It says the city will be captured. A tough message, told straight.

The answer is that he ought to die. The officials tell Zedekiah, Judah's king, “This man ought to die…” (Jeremiah 38:4). They say Jeremiah is discouraging the warriors and all the people by speaking such words to them. That's what they put in front of the king.

The answer is “He is in your hands.” Zedekiah says, “He is in your hands, since the king can do nothing to stop you.” (Jeremiah 38:5). A king handing the whole thing over is something to see, friends. I think the officials didn't need to be told twice.

The answer is mud. The cistern, a pit for storing water, “…had no water but only mud, and Jeremiah sank down into the mud.” (Jeremiah 38:6). This is a heavy part of the story, and I think it hurts to picture. Hold on to this one, friends, because help is coming.

The answer is True. Ebed-melech, a court official from Cush, tells the king, “…these men have acted wickedly in all that they have done to Jeremiah the prophet.” (Jeremiah 38:9). He says it to the king himself.

The reason is that there is no more bread in the city. Ebed-melech says Jeremiah will starve “…for there is no more bread in the city.” (Jeremiah 38:9). Down in the mud, I think that sounds dire. Jeremiah's own words had mentioned famine too (Jeremiah 38:2).

The answer is False. Zedekiah does not turn Ebed-melech down. He commands, “Take thirty men from here with you and pull Jeremiah the prophet out of the cistern before he dies.” (Jeremiah 38:10). Ebed-melech speaks up and the king says yes.

The answer is to pad the ropes. Ebed-melech calls, “Put these worn-out rags and clothes under your arms to pad the ropes.” (Jeremiah 38:12). I think those ropes would dig in without it. It's a small, kind detail from a man who thought ahead, and Jeremiah does it.

The answer is False. They pulled him up with the ropes, “And Jeremiah remained in the courtyard of the guard.” (Jeremiah 38:13). Out of the mud is a big win, but he is still there. I'm glad the pit part is over.

The answer is that the king will surely put him to death. Jeremiah answers King Zedekiah, “If I tell you, you will surely put me to death.” (Jeremiah 38:15). He's just been pulled out of a mud pit, so I think I'd hesitate too, friends. And he's being asked to hide nothing.

The answer is that he will not kill Jeremiah or hand him over. Zedekiah swears, “As surely as the LORD lives, who has given us this life, I will not kill you, nor will I deliver you into the hands of these men who are seeking your life.” (Jeremiah 38:16). He does it secretly. That's a big promise.

The answer is burned. If Zedekiah surrenders, Jeremiah says, “…you will live, this city will not be burned down, and you and your household will survive.” (Jeremiah 38:17). The word comes from the LORD God of Hosts, the God of Israel. It comes with an if: if he surrenders to the officers of the king of Babylon.

The answer is False. If he refuses to surrender, Jeremiah says the LORD's word is, “…you yourself will not escape their grasp.” (Jeremiah 38:18). The city would also be burned down. Zedekiah has two paths in front of him.

The answer is the Jews who deserted to the Chaldeans. Zedekiah says, “I am afraid of the Jews who have deserted to the Chaldeans, for the Chaldeans may deliver me into their hands to abuse me.” (Jeremiah 38:19). I think that fear is real to him. He says it right after Jeremiah tells him what surrender would mean.

The answer is True. Jeremiah replies, “They will not hand you over…” (Jeremiah 38:20). Then he urges the king to obey the voice of the LORD so that it may go well with him. He answers the king's fear straight.

The word is deserted. Jeremiah says that if the king refuses to surrender, the women who remain in the palace will say, “Your feet sank into the mire, and they deserted you.” (Jeremiah 38:22). Those are the king's own trusted friends. I think that line would sting.

The answer is True. Jeremiah says, “All your wives and children will be brought out to the Chaldeans.” (Jeremiah 38:23). He adds that the king himself will be seized by the king of Babylon, and the city burned down. It's a heavy word to give a king.

The answer is that Jeremiah is to say he asked not to be sent back to Jonathan's house to die. Zedekiah tells Jeremiah to say, “I was presenting to the king my petition that he not return me to the house of Jonathan to die there.” (Jeremiah 38:26). That's the line Jeremiah is given for the officials. It's a handy one.

The reason is that no one had overheard the conversation. The officials said no more to him, “…for no one had overheard the conversation.” (Jeremiah 38:27). Jeremiah gave them the exact words the king had commanded him to say. Nobody overheard, and that's the reason the text gives.

The answer is captured, and that's the last line of the chapter. “And Jeremiah remained in the courtyard of the guard until the day Jerusalem was captured.” (Jeremiah 38:28). It's what the LORD's word said would happen to the city. This one is hard to read, friends, and I think it lands heavy. But the story isn't over.
